text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London closed lower with the exception of September which bucked the trend to finish up as origin selling subsided. September added $4 to close at $1,775 per tonne, while November gave up $8 to close at $1,740 per tonne.

Easing concerns over Brazilian frost, USDA's restatement of a crop of 28 million bags for Brazil in 1997/98, and a build in NY exchange certified stocks were the main underlying bearish factors. June and July are the frost-danger months in Brazil but so far there has been no crop-damaging freeze in the country's coffee growing areas and according to weather experts chances of a frost in the coming weeks are also slim.

Arabica futures in New York posted moderate gains in extremely thin trading. Traders said the market is likely to remain under pressure until it becomes more apparent that the period of stock increases is over and consumer stocks once again begin to fall.

Symptomatic is that Colombia's National Coffee Growers Federation reduced its production estimate for 1996/97 (October/September) to about 10 million bags, down from the 10.4 million bags forecast earlier. Traders await the monthly Green Coffee Association of New York's stock report for June, due out on Tuesday, July 15. The range of expectations is plus or minus 100,000 bags.
In May, GCA reported stocks of green coffee in US warehouses rose by 122,000 bags, to 1.977 million bags. Stocks in June 1996 fell by 110,000 bags to 2.161 million bags.

COLOMBIA - Colombia's June coffee crop totalled 1.07 million 60-kg bags compared to 858,000 bags the same month last year, the National Coffee Growers Federation said. For the first six months of this year, the harvest was running at 4.7 million bags compared to 5.3 million bags the same period in 1996, according to Federation figures. The latest figures mean that the harvest for the 1996/97 (October/September) coffee year which has now completed three full quarters, is running at 8.3 million 60-kg bags.

The Federation's latest estimate for total production for 1996/97 is 'about' 10 million bags, down from 10.4 million bags forecast earlier in the year. Production for the final quarter, July/September, is seen at 1.5 million bags according to the Federation. If last quarter predictions are fulfilled the final harvest will total 9.8 million bags, slightly below the Federation's worst scenario forecast.

BRAZIL - Brazil exported 998,850 60-kg bags of coffee, ground and in beans, in June, above the 750,954 bags exported in the same month in 1996. This brought total exports since the beginning of 1997 up to 7.56 million bags, almost exactly twice the 3.76 million bags shipped in the first half of 1996.

Under the ACPC retention scheme, Brazil was not to ship more than 6 million bags in the first six months of 1997. The six-month quota was part of an overall Brazilian export allowance of 15 million bags in 1996/97 (July/June). According to FEBEC statistics, total exports in July/June 1996/97 were 16.54 million bags. The June 1997 sales brought total earnings from coffee exports so far this year to $1.38 bln, 247 per cent higher than the $556.78 million earned the same period in 1996.

SPAIN - Spain imported 289,943 bags of coffee in February 1997, 2 per cent less than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning 1997 up to 641,400 bags, 8 per cent more than was imported the same period in 1996.

Total imports in calendar year 1996 rose by 12 per cent to 3.614 million bags. Main suppliers of green coffee in January/February 1997 were Uganda (184,000 vs 161,300 bags), Brazil (100,500 vs 53,900 bags) and Vietnam (72,900 vs 44,400 bags).

The country exported 113,500 bags of coffee in January/February 1997, 14 per cent more than was exported the same period in 1996. Total exports in calendar year 1996 rose by nearly 50 per cent to 599,500 bags.
